headline: Referred proposed roof-mounted wind energy zoning ordinance for review and recommendation after public hearing.
summary: The council held a public hearing on a proposed zoning ordinance to allow roof-mounted wind energy systems in listed zoning districts. Speakers raised concerns about noise, roof strength, height limits, historic districts, and battery storage. The matter was referred for review and recommendation, all in favor.
decisions: Referred the roof-mounted wind energy zoning ordinance for review and recommendation, all in favor.

decision_evidence.quote: Councilor King moved that the matter be referred to the Planning Board for review and recommendation, all in favor.

JOINT PUBLIC HEARING OF THE  
CITY COUNCIL AND THE PLANNING BOARD 
 
A Joint Public Hearing of the Salem City Council and the Planning Board was held in person  on 
Monday, October 19, 2026, at 6: 00 P .M. in accordance with Chapter 40A, Section 5, of the 
Massachusetts General Laws for the purpose of   discussing Ordinance relative to Zoning - Roof-
Mounted wind Energy Systems Ordinance. 
 
Absent were Councilors Prosniewski, Sydoriak, Hapworth, Smith, and Davis 
 
Council President  Alice Merkl presiding 
 
Councilor Varela joined remotely 
 
The following Planning Board Members were present: Chair Kirt Rieder, Vice Chair Sarah Tarbet, 
Zach Caunter, Helen Sides, Josh Turiel, and Graham Wing 
 
Absent were Jonathan Berk, Elena Eimert, and Tom Furey 
 
Also in attendance was Claudia Cunningham, Planner , Department of Planning and Community 
Development

SUMMARY 
 
Ordinance relative to Zoning - Roof-Mounted wind Energy Systems Ordinance  
 
Section 1. Section 3.1 Table of Principal and Accessory is hereby amended by inserting a new use 
in Section E. ACCESSORY USES as follows:  
Use RC R1 R2 R3 B1 B2 B4 B5 BPD I NRCC 
Wind 
Energy 
System, 
Roof-
Mounted 
Y Y Y Y Y Y Y Y Y Y Y 
 
Section 2.  Section 4.1.2 Notes to Table of Dimensional Requirements is hereby amended by 
inserting the line “and roof-mounted wind energy systems” after “medium-scale ground mounted 
solar energy systems” in subsection 8 and by inserting a new subsection 10:  “The limitations on 
height of buildings shall apply to roof-mounted wind energy systems with an additional allowance 
of 5 feet over the maximum height of the building.”  
 
Section 3. Section 10.0, "Deﬁnitions," is hereby amended by inserting the following deﬁnitions in 
alphabetical order:  
Wind Energy: Energy received from the conversion of wind to electricity.  
Wind Energy System: A device or structural design feature, a substantial purpose of which is to 
provide for the collection, storage, and distribution of wind energy for lighting, space heating or 
cooling, electricity generation, or water heating.  
Wind Energy System Rated Nameplate Capacity: The maximum rated output of electric power 
production equipment for a Wind Energy System.  
Wind Energy System Height: The height of the Wind Energy System is measured from the base of 
the system to the tip of the blade at its highest point.  
Wind Energy System, Roof-Mounted: An Active Wind Energy System that is structurally mounted 
to the roof of a building or structure; shall be considered those with a rated nameplate capacity 
less than or equal to 10 kilowatts per turbine, and a height up to twenty (20) feet.

Section 4. Section 6.9.1, is hereby amended by adding the phrase “Wind Energy System, Roof -
Mounted, as deﬁned in Section 10.0, are not considered wind energy facilities as deﬁned in this 
section (Section 6.9).” at the end of the section, so that it shall read as follows:  
 
6.9.1 Purpose. The purpose of this section is to accommodate wind energy facilities in 
appropriate locations, while minimizing any adverse visual, safety, and environmental impacts of 
the facilities. Wind Energy Systems, Roof-Mounted, as deﬁned in Section 10.0, are not considered 
wind energy facilities as deﬁned in this section (Section 6.9).  
 
This ordinance shall take eﬀect as provided by city charter.  
 
Councilor King discusses the existing zoning ordinance and the lack of language on rooftop wind 
in regard to small commercial and residential spaces. As wind works when solar does not, the two 
work well together. The City Council has had conversations around this topic a nd the 2012 
installation of three (3) hybrid solar/wind turbines on the roof of the South Harbor Garage. There 
have been pilot programs on small rooftop wind across the commonwealth. A 2007 study out of 
UMass studied what Salem’s wind resources were. The best spots were around Winter Island and 
Forest River Park. Castle Hill, Betram Field/Salem Hospital, and Mack Park are likely to be a good 
candidates as well. Rooftop wind is not cost eﬀective for all of Salem. Rooftop wind is not terribly 
popular in the United States. Salem is a viable candidate for this technology as we windy winters 
in a coastal community. The  specialized code for new buildings  seeks to be closer to carbon 
neutral. Some developers may not reach this with solar. Challenges to rooftop wind: solar is cost 
eﬀective, the wind resources of individual locations, potential noise and vibration, the structural 
integrity of roof, battery storage, and visibility. Councilor King shares examples of rooftop wind 
on the international level. Focused on turbines that are shaped to mitigate  the 
space/noise/vibration issues. The ordinance seeks to make rooftop wind allowed by right, with a 
ten (10) foot setback from front, side, and rear lot lines, limits on the height (no higher than ﬁve 
[5] feet over the maximum height of the building ), no larger than ten kilowatts (10 KW)/turbine 
and no taller than twenty (20) feet. Currently, assuming that the existing city noise ordinance will 
suﬃce to mitigate noise issues. Regarding properties in local historic districts, the process would 
likely be similar to the existing one for rooftop solar: an application to the Historical Commission 
for a Certiﬁcate of Appropriateness. And there are updates being made to the battery storage at 
the state and municipal level.  
 
Councilor Varela believes that it is a step in the right direction. Wind energy may not be a priority 
but that does not mean that we should allow residents to put resiliency in their own hands.  
 
Councilor Holappa, there has been an opportunity for residents to provide feedback and there is 
a resident of a ﬂat-roofed house in an R2 interested in this, but they are at the height maximum

October 19, 2026  
Page 4 of 7 
 
already. The city’s c urrently allowed uses to exceed height restrictions include spires, towers, 
chimneys, broadcasting and television antennae, ventilators, roof mounted solar, etc. Should roof 
mounted wind be considered diﬀerently than those uses ? Councilor King says that there were 
conversations around this and feels you could add language to this or the way it was proposed in 
the presentation.  
 
Councilor Flynn thinks that they need to be careful in doing the ordinance as it will change the 
look of Salem. Concerns surrounding noise, the stability of the roof, particularly during storms, 
and how this would look in the neighborhoods. Looks forward to the Planning Board’s input. Also 
think that the ordinance should address noise, even if it may be covered in the current noise 
ordinance. Councilor Flynn will be seeking Ward 4 feedback to guide his decision.  
 
Councilor Turowski is concerned about the permitting , as well as the structural integrity of 
buildings. Is there a plan to monitor installations after they are installed ? We are in a marine 
environment where things degrade quickly and wonder if any of the examples shown in the 
presentation reﬂect marine environments. Councilor King says that you need to be in a speciﬁc 
set of circumstances for this to be eﬃcient, this happens to usually be coastal areas but will look 
more into this. On the inspection piece, curious whether or not the zoning ordinance is the 
appropriate spot to put language on inspections. Should we work with the Building Department 
to have procedures in place or another ordinance? Councilor Turowski suggests that a parallel 
ordinance deﬁning standards may be appropriate; one of the models shown required annual 
inspections.  
 
Councilor Holappa agrees about the concerns with noise and structural integrity. Ask how to make 
certain that people who are interested but would be excluded are informed of this as early as 
possible in the process. 
 
Councilor Varela on the load of the structure will be handled through permitting and conﬁdent 
that the Building Department  can manage this . With regard to historic districts, any kind of 
renewable energy is governed by state law . Believe that a Certiﬁcate of Appropriateness would 
be the correct path forward regarding this, as it is with solar. 
 
Councilor Flynn asks for feedback from Fire Prevention or Fire Department to be included as well, 
particularly surrounding battery storage. The department may have an idea of where to best 
locate a turbine on a building to avoid disrupting ﬁreﬁghting needs. 
 
Councilor Varela states that right now, the state has guidance on battery storage and what is 
appropriate and safe.  
 
PLANNING BOARD COMMENTS 
 
Mr. Turiel thinks some things need to be deﬁned better  and believes a mbient noise standards 
should be included. He  doesn’t really know how many of these we will see on homes, maybe on

October 19, 2026

some of the taller and larger buildings. Questions whether this needs to be regulated if they are 
within the same category as chimneys?  
 
Ms. Sides ﬁnds noise to be less of a concern  as many homes have added condensers on their 
houses, creating noise. Agrees with Mr. Turiel that this is likely better suited for commercial 
properties and new construction, somethig integrated into their overall power plan. The Planning 
Board carefully reviews things on rooftops and tries to be careful about the visibility. Curious as 
to why it could not be a mast or up against the house. The electricity could be brought to the 
ground level. Doesn’t like that this would create more panels on buildings, particularly in the 
historic districts. The Historical Commission will not wai ve a project through solely based on it 
being for energy use . Aesthetically does not like the idea of the turbines on pitched roofs  and 
thinks that speciﬁc models will need to be selected  that are acceptable for the Historical 
Commission. Is in support of anything that provides alternative sources of energy.  Would like to 
see this connected to a pilot program; doesn’t see how individuals could take on the risk and 
aﬀord this; maybe state funding. Councilor King  regarding roof mounted, that is the standard for 
the smaller sized properties and was what she was seeing but is hypothetically open to other 
options. Regarding added noise, just changes in the deﬁnitions would be the closest to staying in 
the four corners. The whole point of the wind energy roof mounted system is to put in restrictions. 
Regarding a pilot program , there is no money right now, but it could be treated like the ADU s 
were a few years ago.  
 
Mr. Wing is concerned that ﬁve (5) feet might be too limiting, especially with buildings that are at 
or exceeding the current allowed height. Thinks allowing latitude would be beneﬁcial. Also thinks 
consideration for a special permit process for exceeding these requirements could be taken on a 
case by case basis.  
 
Ms. Tarbet agrees with Ms. Sides on not limited wall/mass mounted turbines. Agrees with Mr. 
Wing that the ﬁve (5) foot height might be limiting. Wants to make sure that these are reviewed 
carefully. The board has seen projects where the renewable energy plans have not been fully 
ﬂeshed out. And wants to make sure it is part of the site plan review.  
 
Mr. Caunter also has concerns on structural soundness individual rooftops and that there not be 
damage to neighbor properties. Asks if there is a reason why they are limited  the KW/turbine 
output? Equipment could get more eﬃcient in the future. Councilor King says that it was to 
further clarify the distinction between the big turbines and what is considered residential. If what 
people are concerned about is height and size, then maybe the KW restriction is unnecessary. Mr. 
Caunter says yes that neighborhoods like Derby Street would want smaller v. commercial sized 
turbines. 
 
Mr. Rieder is a supporter of wind and quiet revolution vertical access turbines. Speaks to a project 
in another city from a few years ago that wound up not being feasible due to the historic nature 
of the city/area of the proposed project. Wind is often at the edge of a building and thinks this is 
needed to think about. Looking at ordinances in other municipalities , Minneapolis has a

October 19, 2026  
Page 6 of 7 
 
restriction of being three (3) times the height of the device from the property line versus ten (10) 
feet. Most of the presentation’s examples were greater than ﬁve (5) feet tall. One of the examples 
is listed at three (3) feet, but there is a frame on top of that. It needs to be measured to the top 
of the exposed turbine or to the top of the frame. The tree ordinance also has restrictions on the 
removal of public and protected trees. The Tree Commission has observed two landowners who 
have recently removed a number of protected trees. Would like it noted that all other ordinances, 
must be adhered, i.e., Historical Commission and Tree Commission ordinances, so it is not a “we 
are surprised that we couldn’t cut down trees!” Trees reduce the demand and we shouldn’t be 
cutting them down to satisfy wind generation. The technology turns over so quickly  in wind 
energy that projects come and go quickly . The biggest hole is talking about the  height clarity. 
Councilor King the intention of twenty (20) feet of device was end to end total. Thinks that section 
2 is confusing because all we say is “add this line” but could have it say, “so it reads as.”  
 
PUBLIC COMMENT 
 
Josiah Guthrie 
Essex Street 
Brought the issue to Councilors King, Holappa, Varela, and Davis when they realized that wind 
technology was becoming more viable but not allowed in the city. Renewable energy limitations 
for new markets include economic and policy related issues; these  things will become primary 
rather than alternative energy. O n the policy side of things, restrictions are due to lack of 
technology when the ordinance was written. The issues brought up, these are things that the 
industry has been considering. Wind is having a rise with the Archimedes turbine design as it has 
exceeded the theoretical maximum of what could be harvested from wind. Regarding batteries, 
whenever you have energy storage, the is a bit of a loss. Beneﬁt of wind is that there is an inverse 
relationship with solar energy. When we are able to produce energy at all times of the day, that 
is enabling battery systems to be less expensive and safer. There is strength in the versatility of 
wind in the idea of an “energy guild” where the beneﬁts of each renewable energy source are 
stacked to support each other as technology changes. When faced with climate challenges , we 
need to reimagine what it means to preserve the character of a neighborhood. Some see ugly, 
others see a feeling of hope.  
 
Steve  Kapantais (online) 
20 Wisteria Street 
Doesn’t think this is a massive amount of wind towers on peoples house. The northeast is low in 
producing wind. Doesn’t make ﬁnancial sense right now. When addressing noise, need to 
consider decibels and the frequency. Low frequency allows noise  to travel farther. None of this 
will work without batteries as wind is more prevalent in the evenings.  
 
 
 
Councilor King moved to close the public hearing,  all in favor
